pitch.short: I co-founded a campus notebook startup and closed it once postage ate the margin. After that I spent four years at Pinewick Paper & Print in Larchmont Falls, running the day-to-day launch work for a new town counter, and then joined the Alderwick Stationery founder's office to build its weekly review.
why_hire: I have run a small company from purchasing to the bank balance. Quillfold took 1,900 orders and $41,000 of sales before I closed it and published why.
I open new things and stay accountable for the result. At Pinewick I ran operations for the Marlow Cross print counter: 640 business accounts live in 14 weeks, 58% reordering within 30 days.
I build routines that outlive me. During my Alderwick internship I created the weekly review and the quarterly OKRs for six teams, and both are still in use.

about.intro: I grew up in Eastfield and studied commerce at Eastfield University. Midway through the degree a hostel neighbour and I began Quillfold, which printed notebooks and planners for college clubs. It took 1,900 orders in 22 months, and I closed it because each mailed order lost money. In 2021 I joined Pinewick Paper & Print in Larchmont Falls, first in sales operations and from 2023 in strategy, where I ran operations for the Marlow Cross print counter. The PGP at Northmere School of Management followed in 2025, and in 2026 I took a ten-week internship at Alderwick Stationery, working next to its founder. When I give a figure, I state its source.
about.now: I am writing a short handbook on meetings that end on time, and collecting the worst agendas I have ever been sent. My old regional manager's whiteboard acronyms are still ahead.

ai-portfolio-agent.context: Larchmont Falls has a volunteer community print club that lends its presses to local clubs and schools. I joined as a Saturday volunteer in 2026.
ai-portfolio-agent.problem: Paper, toner and ink were tracked in three paper notebooks, so nobody knew what was low until it ran out in the middle of a job.
what_i_did: Counted the whole stock room with two volunteers and gave every item a reorder level.
Built one Google Sheet with a row per item, a count column and a status that turns red below the reorder level.
Wrote a short Apps Script that emails the volunteer on duty a weekly list of what to reorder.
Taped a one-page how-to on the stock room door and retired the three notebooks.

decisions.choice: A sheet instead of an app
decisions.why: Volunteers change every month, and everyone already knew how to open a spreadsheet on their phone.

decisions.choice: Reorder levels set from last year's usage
decisions.why: The old notebooks showed what had been used each month, so levels could come from real numbers instead of guesses.

ai-portfolio-agent.learned: The sheet only held because the weekly email named one person. A shared list nobody owned went stale within a fortnight.
ai-portfolio-agent.next: Add a column for supplier lead time so reorder levels can differ by item.

market-khata.context: Teams on the Northmere School of Management venture course have eight weeks to pick a problem, try out a product and present it on demo day. Mine, four people strong, chose small clinics and tuition centres along Ferry Road in Larchmont Falls.
market-khata.problem: Office managers reorder toner and paper by phone, usually after the last cartridge has already run out in the middle of a print job.
what_i_did: Led the team and planned the eight weeks as research first, then prototype, then pitch.
Interviewed 28 office managers and receptionists along Ferry Road (own record).
Made a clickable Glide prototype holding a supply list for each office, with a WhatsApp reorder reminder sent ahead of a stockout.
Ran a three-week pilot with 5 offices using the prototype list (own record).
Pitched on demo day and finished second out of 24 teams.

decisions.choice: Use WhatsApp for reminders rather than writing an app
decisions.why: Every office manager we met already used WhatsApp all day, and none wanted another login for a supplies list.

decisions.choice: Start with clinics and tuition centres only
decisions.why: Both groups print daily and use supplies quickly, so a late reorder is noticed within a few days. Three weeks was therefore enough to see an outcome.

market-khata.learned: Offices trusted the reminders only after the receptionist agreed to them first. Tilly Brandt at Pinewick had told me this years earlier: the front desk decides what the building uses.

cloud-kitchen-pnl.context: A Northmere School of Management live project with Kettleby Bakery Supplies, a Larchmont Falls firm that delivers flour, packaging and trays to cafes on six routes.
cloud-kitchen-pnl.problem: With a single company-level statement, the firm could not tell which routes were profitable after fuel, driver hours and discounts.
cloud-kitchen-pnl.my_role: Team member, 3 people; built the route P&L model
what_i_did: Pulled invoice and fuel-card data by route for the last two quarters.
Produced a profit statement per route covering revenue, product cost, packaging, fuel, driver hours and discounts, six routes in all.
Found two routes losing money on every drop once fuel and driver hours were counted.
Presented the route P&L to the owner with one recommendation per route.

decisions.choice: Split depot costs by number of drops
decisions.why: Rent and loading staff are shared by all routes. Splitting by drops kept the comparison fair and easy for the owner to check.

decisions.choice: Recommend a fix for each route, not only closures
decisions.why: One route had steady volume and lost money purely through discounting, so reducing those was cheaper than closing it.

results.note: arithmetic, from invoice and fuel data

cloud-kitchen-pnl.learned: The owner acted within days because every row of the model ended in a choice he could make by himself.

monday-review.context: I started The Short Meeting in August 2025, during the PGP, after years of sitting in meetings that ran well past the agenda.
monday-review.problem: Most writing about meetings is general advice. I wanted the real agenda and the one chart from people who run a recurring meeting every week.
what_i_did: Send out an issue each fortnight, every one based on a single conversation with a manager or chief of staff.
Ask every guest for their real agenda, their one chart and the topic they banned.
Spoken with 14 managers and chiefs of staff to date (own record).
Grew the list to 1,400 subscribers without paid promotion (own record).

decisions.why: One person's real meeting teaches more than a roundup of tips.
Booking and writing up one conversation takes about a fortnight, and a weekly issue would have read as padding.

results.note: own record, from the Substack dashboard
own record, from the Substack dashboard

monday-review.learned: Issues carrying the guest's real agenda got forwarded most, so that is now the first thing I request.

threadly-operating-cadence.context: Alderwick Stationery, based in Ashgrove, makes planners and desk supplies and sells through a web shop and a growing number of retail stands. In 2026 six teams answered to the founder, and only the Monday meeting brought them together.
threadly-operating-cadence.problem: Every team arrived with slides using its own definitions. Meetings lasted nearly three hours, nobody wrote decisions down, and just 38% of Monday's agreed actions were finished by the following Monday.
threadly-operating-cadence.my_role: Founder's Office Intern; owned the review and the OKR cycle
what_i_did: Watched three reviews and noted each topic along with its length and whether anything was decided. 54% of the time went on debating what the figures meant.
Settled 12 common metrics with the six team leads, then put them in a single Looker Studio dashboard fed by the current Sheets and web-shop data.
Swapped slides for a Notion page per team holding three numbers, the main change and any request for the founder.
Fixed the agenda at 55 minutes and tracked actions in a Slack log, each with a named owner and a due date.
Led the Q3 OKRs: wrote the company objectives alongside the founder, then refined each lead's key results until one person owned every one.

decisions.choice: Settle the figures before the meeting
decisions.why: Most of the time went to disputes over definitions. With one dashboard as the only source, the meeting could open on decisions.

decisions.choice: One page per team, sent the evening before
decisions.why: The founder already read updates on Sunday evening. Taking that reading out of the meeting itself saved the most minutes.

results.note: mean of the final 4 weeks; leadership-confirmed, not audited
7-week period, counted from the action log in Slack; own record

threadly-operating-cadence.learned: Building the dashboard took two weeks. Getting six leads to accept one meaning of 'on-time order' took three. The routine held once the founder stopped taking slides into the room.
threadly-operating-cadence.next: Add a monthly review for the retail stands, since their figures shift too slowly for a weekly look.

activation-tracker.context: In 2022 I was an Operations Associate in Pinewick's sales operations team, handling bulk print quotes for business customers from request to sent price.
activation-tracker.problem: Quote status lived in four spreadsheets, a stack of sticky notes at the front desk and many Slack threads. An open quote often had no clear owner, and a median quote in my team took 5.8 days.
activation-tracker.my_role: Operations Associate; designed and built the tool
what_i_did: Mapped every step from quote request to sent price with two team leads and marked where requests waited.
Created one Airtable base in which every quote carries a stage, an owner and a follow-up.
Set up Zapier to message Slack whenever a quote stays in the same stage past two days.
Retired the four spreadsheets, apart from one of Dennis Hale's, which he kept on principle, and helped three more teams adopt the tracker.

decisions.choice: Use Airtable and Zapier instead of queuing for IT
decisions.why: IT would have taken a full quarter just to start. The no-code tool was working before the quarter ended, and the team could edit it without help.
Most delays came from handoffs where each person assumed someone else was chasing the customer.

results.note: sales, accounts and warehouse; own record

thistledown-launch.context: In 2023 Pinewick Paper & Print wanted to know whether small businesses outside Larchmont Falls would buy printing and stationery from a same-day counter instead of driving to the city. Marlow Cross was the first test town.
thistledown-launch.problem: Nothing existed to follow. We had not decided which trade districts to start in, how many field reps to hire, or what would make a new account keep ordering.
thistledown-launch.my_role: Strategy and Operations Associate; ran the launch
what_i_did: Mapped 11 trade districts in Marlow Cross by business density and type, and picked four to start in: Tannery Lane, Mill Street, Ferry Road and Ashdown Square.
Recruited and trained seven field reps together with the town manager, with daily visit goals for each district.
Managed account set-up through one shared tracker and a WhatsApp group for every district, and repaired the three stages at which credit checks stalled.
Phoned 96 accounts that went quiet in month one and categorised their reasons.
Turned the Marlow Cross data into a launch playbook that the Hollin Bridge team then followed.

decisions.choice: Start with solicitors' and accountants' offices
decisions.why: Contracts and filings are printed weekly there, so speed counted for much more than for a shop needing one flyer monthly.

decisions.choice: A week-2 delivery check for every new account
decisions.why: Accounts that lapsed had nearly always hit trouble within two weeks, typically a delivery that missed its slot. Wendell Odom's warehouse crew nicknamed these 'the lost Tuesday'. A check at week 2 caught them early.

results.note: compared with 39% during launch month one; own record
vs 14 for Marlow Cross, using the playbook; own record

thistledown-launch.learned: Retention was settled in the first fortnight. Accounts whose first delivery arrived on time and matched the order mostly stayed; the others mostly left. Marla Finch bet me lunch that we would miss the week-10 target. She paid.

city-launch-playbook.context: Marlow Cross was the first test town for Pinewick's print counters. In 2024 the branch growth team chose Hollin Bridge as the second and wanted it open sooner.
city-launch-playbook.problem: Opening Marlow Cross took 14 weeks, and the lessons sat in my spreadsheets and the field team's chat groups.
city-launch-playbook.my_role: Strategy and Operations Associate; author of the playbook
what_i_did: Authored the town launch playbook from Marlow Cross figures, covering how to choose districts, how large the field team should be, what to aim for each day and the account set-up checklist.
Added fixes for the three credit-check steps where Marlow Cross accounts got stuck.
Made the week-2 delivery check a rule for every new account, with the reasons from 96 calls to accounts that had stopped ordering.
Walked the Hollin Bridge town manager through the playbook before opening day.

decisions.choice: Base it on the call log, not recollection
decisions.why: Ninety-six calls produced reasons that could be tallied, letting the playbook put the important steps first.
In Marlow Cross it caught most early delivery problems before accounts went back to driving to the city.

results.note: vs 14 for Marlow Cross; own record

results.value: Used for the Hollin Bridge launch

second-sem.context: Club treasurers at Eastfield University and two nearby colleges wanted notebooks and planners with their logo on the cover, on a tiny budget. I founded Quillfold with a hostel neighbour in August 2019, partway through our degree.
second-sem.problem: Printing notebooks and handing them over at campus tables was cheap. What we did not know was whether the model would survive once most orders came from far away and needed posting.
second-sem.my_role: Co-founder; ran purchasing, operations and finance
what_i_did: Bought plain notebooks in bulk from a paper wholesaler and printed club covers ourselves on a second-hand press.
Sold at a Friday pickup table on three campuses plus a web shop, logging orders first in Google Sheets and later in Shopify.
Reviewed profit per order monthly, separating pickup orders from posted ones.
When COVID closed the campuses in 2020, club orders stopped. We spent six months selling to alumni groups by post, which pushed postage costs up further.
Shut the business in June 2021 after paying all volunteers and suppliers, and posted a post-mortem with the figures.

decisions.choice: Leave pickup free but bill for postage
decisions.why: Pickup orders made $4.10 each; mailed orders lost money. A $3 postage charge halved the number of mailed orders.
Growth could only come from posted orders, and each of those lost $2.30 after returns. Extra funding would simply have lost money more quickly.

results.note: after postage, packaging and 12% returns; arithmetic

second-sem.learned: Margin by channel should have been on my sheet in month one. For nearly a year we cheered order growth that came from the losing channel.
